title: Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November
full_text: Sep 23, 2026 7:03am PT Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November By Jem Aswad Plus Icon Jem Aswad Executive Editor, Music jemaswad Latest Bad Brains’ Earliest Studio Recordings to Be Released in November 6 minutes ago Warner Chappell Co-Chair/COO Carianne Marshall to Step Down From Post 2 days ago Sesame Street Transforms Chappell Roan’s ‘Hot to Go!’ Into the Potty-Training Anthem ‘Got to Go,’ With Lead Vocals From Cookie Monster 5 days ago See All As anyone reading this probably knows, the Bad Brains were one of the most important punk-rock bands of all time, Washington D.C.-bred pioneers of the sound that became hardcore. While they were a complete anomaly at the time — four Black dudes in an overwhelmingly white music scene who seasoned their blistering rock songs with impressively authentic reggae — their impact was immediate and immense. While the group was as fractious interpersonally as they were musically — they split up many times, usually when they were on the verge of a breakthrough — their early albums and particularly their explosive live shows contain some of the most powerful rock music of the ‘80s. They are considered by many to be the greatest hardcore band of all time; Dave Grohl has said he learned how to play drums by bashing on pillows along with their records, and a mural of the band was painted in 2024 across the street from the site of their frequent haunt CBGB in New York. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ A Graffiti Mural incorporating Glen E. Friedman’s artwork celebrating the punk rock band Bad Brains on the corner of Bleeker Street and Bowery is shown in a photograph taken on October 24, 2024 in New York City. (Photo by Al Pereira/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images) Getty Images The group’s catalog is about to get an addition that is both old and new: On November 6, just in time to join the insurrection that will surely follow the midterm elections, a little-known recording of their first session in a proper studio will be released as “Are You Ready: The First Studio Recordings.” While an early demo recording was release in 1996 as the “Black Dots” album, this six-song session, recorded in an hour at Inner Ear Studios in March 1979, predates even that by three months. Popular on Variety The recordings were remixed by Minor Threat/ Fugazi co-founder and longtime friend Ian MacKaye — who has been on an archival binge recently, having worked with Henry Rollins to restore the catalog of psychobilly legends the Cramps — and will be available on vinyl, cassette, and digital. The EP joins the group’s full catalog, much of which was out of circulation for many years but recently got a proper reissue treatment and now is available on streaming services. It includes a previously unreleased recording of the band’s legendary debut single, “Pay to Cum,” which is released today with video footage filmed ay CBGB in October of 1979. “The riff for ‘Pay to Cum’ started as a stream of punk rock vibes fueled by the Ramones, the Damned, and Return to Forever,” says Bad Brains bassist Darryl Jenifer, reflecting the band’s unusual combination of inlfuences. “It was a gift that served as a springboard into our sound – sheer, straight-ahead three-chord mayhem with a few breaks and a stop. The title actually meant nothing to us; it was just a fun-loving play on words.” Listen/share “Pay to Cum” here and watch the video – with footage was filmed by Barry Masterson at CBGB’s October 24th 1979. On November 5, a day before the album’s release, Jenifer and Ian will appear in conversation at the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, discussing the session and the band’s formative years. From November 6 through the 22nd, an exhibition of archival Bad Brains material will open, featuring contributions from the archives of Darryl Jenifer, Alison Braun, BJ Papas, Lucien Perkins, Alec MacKaye, Roger Gastman, and more. Blue Man Group’s A New Holiday Surprise , described as an “all-new festive spectacular,” will begin performances at the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre on November 12, with an official opening night set for November 17. The strictly limited run will play through January 3, 2027. A New Holiday Surprise marks the Group’s first-ever touring holiday production, with the New York stop its first-ever Broadway staging. title: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Could Top Box Office, Brad Pitt’s ‘Heart of the Beast’ and Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ Vie for No. 3
full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:50am PT ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Could Top Box Office, Brad Pitt’s ‘Heart of the Beast’ and Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’ Vie for No. 3 By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest ‘Evita’ on Broadway: West End Stars Diego Rodriguez, James Olivas to Reprise Roles Alongside Rachel Zegler (EXCLUSIVE) 23 hours ago Box Office: ‘Resident Evil’ Breaks Franchise Records With $60 Million Opening Weekend 3 days ago ‘Backrooms’ Surpasses $400 Million at Global Box Office 3 days ago See All ©Walt Disney Co./courtesy Everett / Everett Collection In a blast from the past, “Avengers: Endgame” might actually wind up as No. 1 at the domestic box office in… 2026. Disney is bringing the Marvel juggernaut back to the big screen ahead of “Avengers: Doomsday,” which opens in December. The 2019 superhero adventure is tracking to collect $25 million to $28 million over the weekend, a sizable haul for a re-release. “Avengers: Endgame Encore” will compete for first place against Zach Cregger’s reboot of “ Resident Evil ,” which is targeting $24 million to $26 million in its sophomore outing. “Resident Evil” topped last weekend’s box office with $61 million, a franchise-best debut. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ Meanwhile, three new releases — Paramount’s Brad Pitt-led survival adventure “The Heart of the Beast ,” Universal and DreamWorks Animation’s family friendly “Forgotten Island” and A24’s “To Catch a Predator”-inspired “ Primetime ,” starring Robert Pattinson — will vie for third place. “Primetime” and “The Heart of the Beast” are each projected to debut to $17 million to $20 million, while “Forgotten Island” is aiming for $15 million to $17 million. All three newcomers have great reviews and could exceed expectations with positive word-of-mouth. Popular on Variety “Primetime” cost just $15 million to produce, so the movie is well-positioned to turn a profit in its theatrical run. “The Heart of the Beast” and “Forgotten Island,” by comparison, were much more expensive to make. “The Heart of the Beast” carries an $82 million price tag and “Forgotten Island” was produced for $80 million, so those films will need to stick around on the big screen beyond opening weekend to justify their sizable budgets. (That’s because theater owners get to keep roughly 50% of ticket sales.) “Primetime” continues a banner year for Pattinson, who starred in the spring indie hit “The Drama,” Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” and will appear in Denis Villeneuve’s upcoming “Dune: Part III.” Directed by Lance Oppenheim, “Primetime” follows Pattinson as Dateline NBC journalist Chris Hansen and revolves around the production of the popular series “To Catch a Predator,” in which he attempted to confront child sexual predators in complex sting operations. Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo and Phoebe Bridgers round out the cast of “Primetime,” which bowed at Venice Film Festival to raves. “Heart of the Beast” was directed by David Ayer and stars Pitt as a retired veteran who navigates a brutal 58-mile trek to safety after he and his trusted combat dog survive a harrowing plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness. Hollywood will be closely watching “Heart of the Beast” because it’s being released just days after Paramount settled an antitrust case with state attorneys general that removed a major obstacle to closing its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount’s CEO David Ellison has pledged to release at least 30 new films a year through the joint company — but exhibitors want to make sure those movies will bring out audiences. “Forgotten Island,” which revolves around two best friends who get stranded in a mystical world, could benefit from pent-up demand; there hasn’t been a major kid-centric movie since “Moana” in July. Plus, recent animated movies like “The Wild Robot,” “GOAT” and “Minions & Monsters” managed to remain big screen draws in the weeks after their debuts. “Forgotten Island” was directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado and counts H.E.R., Dave Franco and Jenny Slate among the voice cast. “Avengers: Endgame,” which needs no introduction, looms as the second-biggest movie in box office history with $2.799 billion worldwide. Excitement for the re-release certainly bodes well for “Avengers: Doomsday,” which unites nearly all of Earth’s Mightiest Heroes and is predicted to be one of the biggest movies of 2026. Right now, Sony’s Marvel sequel “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” ranks as this year’s largest domestic debut with $360 million and highest-grossing worldwide release with $2.47 billion. title: Production Surge in Spain Confirmed by Olsberg SPI Study, but Headwinds Approach
full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:45am PT Production Surge in Spain Confirmed by Olsberg SPI Study, but Headwinds Approach Said Spain Film Commission's Juan Manuel Guimeráns: ‘If the U.S. introduces a federal tax credit, I expect production there to grow. I don’t think that’s necessarily negative for other territories. If production in the U.S. increases, labor and other costs may rise, which could still push some production elsewhere’ By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest ‘Fluorescent, Dirty and Sexy’: Eire Cid’s ‘The Imaginary Kings’ Presented at Madrid Film School (ECAM) Incubator 9 hours ago Queer Horror Explored in ECAM Incubator Title ‘The Unmoving Hands’ 21 hours ago El Sol Ermitaño Launches at San Sebastián Festival With WIP Title ‘Lovers Go Home’ (EXCLUSIVE) 21 hours ago See All (l-r) Marta Moretto, Olsberg SPI; Kayleigh Hughes, Olsberg SPI; Jesus Cambra, Pablo de Olavide University; Xiomara Garcia, Film Madrid Region; Rodrigo Diaz, SEDIA; Juan Manuel Guimeráns, Spain Film Commission Courtesy of Spain Film Commission Spain’s audiovisual sector is continuing to expand, with production spend expected to reach €5.68 billion ($6.6 billion) in 2025, up 45% from 2022, according to a new study by U.K.-based consultancy Olsberg SPI , commissioned by the Spain Film Commission . At a presentation held at the San Sebastian Festival, Kayleigh Hughes of Olsberg SPI said the study expands on the consultancy’s 2024 analysis of incentivized international production, taking a broader look at Spain’s audiovisual production sector from 2023-25. Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ The research uses Spanish Statistical Institute data to measure production expenditure across film, video and television, including spending on goods, services and personnel. However, it excludes exhibition, distribution, broadcasting and video games, while post-production will be included in the full report, she added. Popular on Variety The sector is expected to generate €4.98 billion in gross value added (GVA) for the Spanish economy in 2025. That includes €2.72 billion in direct activity, alongside indirect activity generated by suppliers and service providers and induced activity linked to employee spending. Hughes said the figures underline the audiovisual sector’s growing economic footprint beyond production companies themselves, supporting a wider ecosystem of businesses and workers. The study also points to broader benefits including screen tourism, cultural visibility, technical innovation and sustainability. Spain has also recorded strong growth in film and co-production volumes in recent years, according to European Audiovisual Observatory data, reinforcing its position as both a domestic production hub and an international filming destination. A panel comprising Spain Film Commissioner Juan Manuel Guimeráns, Madrid Film Region Coordinator Xiomara Garcia, Olsberg SPI’s Marta Moretto and Jesus Cambra of the Pablo De Olavide University held forth on the current state of affairs. Moretto said the figures in the Olsberg study reflect substantial public and private investment and underline the growing scale of Spain’s production ecosystem. The sector’s economic impact extends well beyond production companies. Jesús Cambram of Pablo de Olavide University noted that almost half of the roughly €5 billion in value generated around the audiovisual industry is created outside the sector itself, demonstrating its wider “tractor effect.” The employment multiplier is similarly significant: for every 10 jobs directly linked to audiovisual production, another 11 are generated outside the sector, Cambram asserted. Those jobs include electricians, carpenters, hair and makeup professionals, transport workers and hospitality staff. “We’re not talking only about production,” Cambram said. “There are many more activities that benefit from the positive momentum of the audiovisual industry.” He argued that workforce training should reflect those needs, with skills shortages in areas such as electrical work and carpentry potentially affecting production while also creating opportunities across the wider economy. Guimeráns, meanwhile, stressed that the sector’s impact extends to wages and working conditions beyond the audiovisual workforce. “Touching this sector is either doing good or doing harm to other sectors,” he said, urging policymakers to consider those knock-on effects when designing measures affecting production. The territorial impact is particularly visible in Madrid, where the regional audiovisual industry generates around 30,000 jobs, according to Garcia of the Madrid Film Regional Office. She said productions increasingly depend on local infrastructure, suppliers and services, making municipalities important parts of the production ecosystem. She cited a shoot at a protected 18th-century theater that required specialist carpenters and technicians while also benefiting local restaurants. In another example, “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon” used an 8,000-square-meter production hub and hired a specialist vintage-car restoration company to prepare vehicles for the production. Guimeráns said Spain is now among the leading audiovisual markets in the E.U. in absolute terms, but faces competition both internationally and between its own regions. “The producer moves very easily,” he said. “The territories and sectors that have better conditions attract more activity.” He singled out the potential impact of new U.S. production incentives and warned that even policy announcements can influence production decisions. For Spain, he argued that any reform should improve incentives while preserving the mechanisms that are already working. “We have to improve Spanish incentives — not only in percentage, but also in procedures, legal certainty and timing,” Guimeráns said. “Let’s do it, but let’s do it with a clear head.” Spain’s growing production base, he added, is producing films, series and television formats that are increasingly traveling internationally. “What we have to do is push that forward,” he said. “The study’s 2025 estimates show investment stabilizing after significant growth between 2022 and 2024,” Guimeráns later told Variety, adding that the slowdown reflects intensifying international competition. “The jump from 2022 to 2023 coincided with Spain’s improved tax incentives,” he said. “Since then, other countries have been changing their incentives too — Italy, Portugal, France and the U.K. We’re all fishing in the same pond. It’s a big pond with room to grow, but we’re all fishing in it.” But incentives are only one factor in production decisions. “Production doesn’t move from one territory to another for a single reason,” Guimeráns said. “Incentives are important, of course, but so are labor and production costs and how easy it is to shoot in a particular territory.” He said historical data suggests incentives tend to expand the overall production market, even if activity shifts between territories. “If the U.S. introduces a federal tax credit, I expect production there to grow,” he told Variety. “I don’t think that’s necessarily negative for other territories. If production in the U.S. increases, labor and other costs may rise, which could push some production elsewhere.” Among recent major productions in Spain, Guimeráns highlighted “The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon” calling it “a very powerful, very large production” with filming spread across the country. title: ‘Variations on Violence’ Wins Best Film at Oldenburg
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:42am 'Variations on Violence' Courtesy of the Oldenburg Film Festival Zachary Nichols’ Variations on Violence won the German Independence Award for Best Film at this year’s Oldenburg Film Festival, Germany’s leading indie film festival. The film follows a military drone operator whose remote-controlled violence follows him home, along with his sister Mary, who is caught in a cycle of unstable relationships as Johnny’s grip on reality deteriorates. Nichols originally developed the project as an art installation before expanding it into a feature. Boris Mojsovski’s Foreign Tongue received the Spirit of Cinema Award, which is determined by festival audience vote. The Canadian film, in its German premiere, stars Steve Byers, Cynthia Aspherger and Greg Bryk. It centers on Kathy (Kim Sue Murray) a single woman who falls into a coma after a fall at a speed-dating event and wakes up speaking with a Bosnian accent — a change that alters how she is perceived and treated, and that connects her with a hospital cleaner who introduces her to a new social world. Related Stories TV Jeff Probst Reveals Major 'Survivor 51' Twist -- and It Could Change the Game for Years (Exclusive) TV New Documentaries-Only Streamer DocuStream Sets Launch Plans (Exclusive) Marjorie Conrad’s The Joyless Economy won the German Independence Award for Originality, Daring and Audacity. The 58-minute film is built from the video collection of an unnamed woman and follows her sexual history and infidelities in a split-screen structure, pairing her cinematic tastes, particularly her growing porn obession, on one side of the frame with her life story on the other. The Oldenburg jury called the film “hypnotic and ethically complex.” The Joyless Economy premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight section. Matthew Osubor’s Big Daddy’s Flowers received the Hans Ohlms Award for Best Debut Film. The jury noted the film, which had its world premiere at Oldenburg, was made without a budget and praised the resourcefulness that constraint produced, comparing its tone to the irreverence of 1990s comedies. Osubor, who also stars, made the film under the mentorship of 90s indie film stalwart Alexandre Rockwell ( In the Soup ) follows an ambitious flower-delivery driver (Osubor) who gets drawn into the orbit of a powerful local figure called Big Daddy. Matthew Osubor in Big Daddy’s Flowers. Courtesy of the Oldenburg Film Festival The Seymour Cassel Award for acting went to Frank Mosley for Jackrabbit and Gia Crovatin for Murderous . Mosley was recognized for his role as T.A. Diamond in Jared Hogan’s film, set in 1930s Utah, about a miner disabled in an accident who leaves his family under false pretenses with a hidden revolver. The jury called the performance non-performative, saying it reflected honesty and authenticity within a bleak setting while retaining the character’s humanity and humor. Crovatin was honored for her role as Marian, a filmmaker accused of creative theft by a former classmate, in Neil LaBute’s Murderous , a psychological thriller LaBute has said drew on Joseph L. Mankiewicz’s Sleuth and Alfred Hitchcock’s Rope and Dial M for Murder . The jury noted the difficulty of embodying dialogue-driven material and called the performance an achievement within that tradition. The 107-minute film, co-starring Thomas Sodaski and Jordan Baker, had its world premiere at the Globe Oldenburg. Gia Crovatin in Murderous . Courtesy of the Oldenburg Film Festival Michele Leonardi’s White Whiter Whitest Black won the German Independence Award for Best Short Film. The jury praised the 15-minute film’s restraint, saying it trusted its audience without over-explaining, and described it as addressing themes of innocence and guilt through a betrayal the jury called difficult to reconcile morally, handled with simplicity. This year’s retrospective was dedicated to LaBute , who attended alongside Crovatin. The festival screened LaBute’s In the Company of Men (1997), Your Friends & Neighbors , Nurse Betty (2000), Some Velvet Morning (2013) and House of Darkness (2022) in conjunction with the retrospective. Stunt performer Zoe Bell received a tribute in recognition of more than three decades of work in the field; the festival screened Double Dare (2004), Death Proof (2007), Angel of Death (2009) and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) as part of the program. title: Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc Drops Full Trailer — and You Will Want to See Everything
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 23, 2026 6:37am 'You Can See Everything' A24 In Nathan Fielder ‘s documentary film about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes , you can see everything — including Holmes shed a(t least one) tear. On Wednesday, A24 released the full-length trailer (below) for You Can See Everything from Fielder ( Nathan for You , The Rehearsal ) and Lance Oppenheim . It’s crazy, it’s confusing, it’s uncomfortable — but that’s Nathan for you. The new film will release in theaters on Oct. 16 following its brief festival tour. You Can See Everything has joined the New York Film Fest Spotlight Lineup , where it will debut on Sept. 30. The film already enjoyed a surprise world premiere at Telluride — that’s where all of those critics’ pull quotes came from. Related Stories Movies Inside NYFF's Splashy Lineup: Landing 'Artificial,' Weighing a Secret Screening and Opening on the "Miraculous" 'Paper Tiger' (Exclusive) TV 'Crystal Lake' Trailer Sends Linda Cardellini's Pam Voorhees Over the Edge The trailer is a bit more revealing than what we got last time from a brief teaser, but like Fielder and Holmes, everything here still presents as an enigma wrapped in a mystery. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s critic, Angie Han, wrote that You Can See Everything “begins as a fascinatingly intimate portrait of a deluded or disingenuous scammer reveals as something even wilder, more ambitious and less predictable, until we’re left to ponder what value a personal truth has at all.” You Can See Everything is a film in two parts, Han wrote out of Telluride. Its second half kicks into a second fifth gear. “Its abrupt turns are so deliciously surprising I’m loath to give away too much detail,” Han tip-toed. “But I’ll say broadly that it gets excitingly meta and almost surreal in confronting the fact that Holmes is now in prison, and therefore unable to speak for herself in any length or depth. Control of her narrative has once again slipped outside her hands, and in her absence, the void gets filled by other means.” You Can See Everything , created in secret over four years by the directors, provides the billionaire-turned-convicted-fraudster a platform to share her side of the Theranos story. Holmes continuously professed her innocence alongside partner Billy Evans before being hauled off to prison to serve an 11-year sentence. Boiled down to basics, Holmes hyped up her company Theranos as having the ability to run hundreds of health and medical tests using a single drop of blood from a finger prick. Founded in 2003, Theranos eventually reached a $9 billion valuation, but it was almost all smoke and mirrors. Holmes’ proprietary miracle machine, The Edison, could never reliably do what she claimed it could, and the company dissolved in 2018. THR

title: ‘Digger’: Tom Cruise’s “Brave Gorgeous Misfire” Gets Very Mixed First Reactions
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:26am Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy of Warner Bros. Tom Cruise ‘s Digger is being called a very big swing of a dramatic satire that’s provoking mixed-to-negative reactions after the film’s first press screenings. In Digger , Cruise — nearly unrecognizable in makeup and prosthetics — plays an oblivious oil tycoon whose drilling in Greenland dislodges an ice shelf from a glacier that’s going to cause a global disaster. He must race to prove that he’s humanity’s savior before the ecological accident wreaks havoc on the planet. The film also stars Riz Ahmed, Sandra Hüller, John Goodman, Michael Stuhlbarg and Jesse Plemons. Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Reveals How He Cut 'Digger' Transformation Time From Six Hours to Under One Business Tom Cruise Blesses Paramount's Deal to Buy Warner Bros., in the Name of Movie "Abundance" The apocalyptic film from Alejandro G. Iñárritu is being called everything from “brave” to “baffling” to an outright “misfire” after screenings were held in New York and Los Angeles. The story, which is also drawing comparisons to Dr. Strangelove , also includes a very big reveal — which we won’t spoil — that is getting strong reactions from the crowd. Still, many critics expect Digger will be a strong awards contender, particularly for Cruise’s performance and the film’s production design, but also expect Warner Bros. and Legendary to have a very tough time recouping their estimated $130 million investment (“I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore,” one critic predicted). Here are some of the first reactions: Anne Thompson (IndieWire): “A.G. Iñárritu’s Digger is a brave and gorgeous art film that will not score with mainstream audiences but will play best for the Academy, especially crafts and actors. But critics will divide on Cruise. The tour-de-force amphitheater scene might put him across. Riz Ahmed is fab.” Ryan Lattanzio (Screen Talk): “The problem with continuing to make statements about your own art and reflect on your own legacy is that you’ll eventually ruin both. A self-indulgent miscalculation from end to end.” Mike Ryan : “Tom Cruise, as you probably expect, is *going for it* in DIGGER, which makes me want to like it. Though I find some plot choices baffling. There are very interesting moments in a meta, Cruise’s career way, but MAVERICK did them better. (It’s also kind of generally unpleasant.)” Edward Douglas (The Weekend Warrior Show): “I cannot say that Digger is very good, although I could tell what Iñarritu and Cruise were going for. There is a major reveal (not a twist) towards the end that almost justifies the craziness… but it will be a tough movie to review, and I expect a HORRENDOUS CinemaScore.” Chris Gore (Film Threat): “ Digger is the biggest swing of Cruise’s career. It’s either going to blow your mind or you’ll have other thoughts when you learn what is really happening in Iñárritu’s masterfully directed film.” Hoai-Tran Bui (Inverse): “Very mixed on DIGGER which had things I liked (Cruise’s performance included) and things I found absolutely insufferable. I wasn’t a devoted Inarritu hater before this but now I kind of get it!” Matt Neglia (Next Best Picture): “This is Tom Cruise’s most dynamic and interesting role in years, and it provides him plenty of space to preach to the back row but not enough to dig deeper and deliver a performance that could’ve had far more power and nuance had Alejandro González Iñárritu’s ambitious split narrative not been so imbalanced in favor of its zany but empty theatrics. Nobody else is given enough material to fully flesh out their characters … Less of a bang and more of a hollow misfire.” Joey Magidson (Awards Radar): “Digger is a mess. Tom Cruise and Alejandro G. Iñárritu are taking a massive swing here, but despite some great production design and a commitment to their big choices, not a whole lot works here. Cruise is good and Riz Ahmed is a highlight, but man this wasn’t enjoyable.” Scott Menzel : “Alejandro González Iñárritu continues to take big swings and make bold choices as a writer and filmmaker. While this film certainly won’t work for everyone, I found the pairing of Iñárritu and Tom Cruise to be an engaging and one of a kind experience. Cruise really does have a knack for comedy, and while not all the jokes land, he fully commits to his performances and the material…This is very much the type of film that will take a bit of time to process after you see it … Digger is ambitious, messy and strange, but it is also a film that will be incredibly divisive and get people talking. It does what good art should do so even if it’s not a perfect film.” Clayton Davis ( Variety ): “ Digger is not what people are expecting — and how audiences react may be the ultimate test of Tom Cruise’s star power. I respect the swing and what Alejandro González Iñárritu is going for. Tom Cruise and John Goodman are delivering stellar work (Sophie Wilde might be best in show for me), and the production design and cinematography are impressive (we’ve missed you, Chivo). In the end, not all the dots connect, and I wish the film leaned harder into the absurdity and satire it kept reaching for. Shocker! The divide on this one is going to be wide.” Jack Hamilton ( Good Day Chicago ): “DIGGER is my favorite film of ‘26 — I avoided spoilers, so the surprises had an incredible impact. A bit Kubrick, a bit BLACK MIRROR but also feels original — a surreal, weird, funny study on (human) nature and storytelling. Tom Cruise’s performance ranks among his career best.” Kristen Lopez (The Film Maven): “DIGGER is a very mixed bag. You’ll get what it’s saying, and the concept is interesting, but it doesn’t trust the audience enough not to hold its hand. Riz Ahmed is great. The Cruise performance is solid. Hard to do satire when the absurdity is so prominent in reality.” Digger opens in theaters Oct. 2. THR

title: Meet One of the Key Republicans Championing a Federal Film and TV Tax Credit
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:25am Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) speaks to supporters of President Donald Trump at an event hosted by Vice President JD Vance on August 21, 2025 in Peachtree City, Georgia. Megan Varner/Getty Images Hollywood is stereotypically seen as an industry beloved and supported by liberal politicians, but the current push for a federal film and television tax credit is complicating that typical portrait. Even before President Donald Trump ordered Congress to “get this done!” on Aug. 31, a few key conservative backers of the incentive idea, working alongside Jon Voight , unions and studios alike, emerged in the legislative branch, U.S. Rep. Brian Jack (R-GA) among them. A 38-year-old freshman Congressman representing an area of Georgia that stretches from the suburbs of Atlanta to the border with Alabama, Jack is in some ways a natural ally to the industry. His district includes Trilith Studios, the sprawling production complex in Fayetteville that has hosted Moana , Superman and multiple Marvel shoots in past years, but was impacted by the latter Disney-owned brand’s recent relocation of major shoots to the U.K. Jack is also, as The Hollywood Reporter learned in a recent interview, a movie props collector. In his possession include several props from his favorite TV show, Entourage , the credit card that Daniel Craig’s James Bond swiped in 2006’s Casino Royale (a gift from Pawn Stars ’ Rick Harrison, Jack is careful to note, before he was elected to Congress) and a business card used by Sebastian Stan’s Bucky Barnes in Thunderbolts* , which was filmed in part at Trilith. “As you may recall, he [Barnes] served as a congressman in Thunderbolts , so I have his congressional business card,” Jack says. Make no mistake, Jack is also an unambiguous Trump-era Republican. Before being elected to the House, Jack served as Trump’s political director during and following his first term in the White House, then joined the office of former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy as a close advisor. Main issues listed on his re-election campaign website include ending illegal immigration, cutting taxes, supporting American energy including oil and gas and ending “the weaponization of justice” against former President Joe Biden’s “perceived enemies.” To understand his interest in a federal tax credit, THR sat down with Jack at his office in Capitol Hill’s Longworth House Office Building, once the domain of former President Lyndon B. Johnson when he was a House representative. Jack explained what the film and television production caucus will do, responded to criticism of the federal tax credit and revealed how he plans on getting more Republicans on board. Why did you decide to take a leadership role in creating and film and television caucus as well as supporting the tax incentive? Well, first and foremost, I am proud to represent Trilith Studios, one of the largest movie production studios in the country. And it’s very special for my district because it not only has generated many, many jobs across my district from craftsmen to carpenters to electricians, but it also is a source of pride for many of us. Many of the movies we see on the big screen are filmed literally in my backyard, so to speak. I grew up in Fayette County, live in Peachtree City, and many of these movies were produced at Trilith Studios in Fayette County. Unfortunately, we’ve seen over the last three to four years, a mass exodus of film production to other countries. I’ve been told, unsure if this is the specific statistic, but I’ve been told that at its peak, occupancy on the lots was 98 percent or close to 100 percent when they were filming Avengers: Endgame . And today occupancy is extremely low, perhaps in the single digits. So it certainly has made an impact on my district and I’m eager to revitalize American film production. I, like President Trump, believe that our country is well served by having a robust film production industry. From everything I’ve heard, you’ve been interested in the incentive idea for a while. Why is an incentive important, in your view, as opposed to more punitive measures like tariffs? Well, I will say from the outset, I have long supported an all-above approach because I think ultimately our common shared goal is for American film production to flourish. And if a punitive measure and action is the most constructive way to achieve that, then I would be supportive of that. If it’s incentives to film in states and generate jobs and grow the economy of communities and states we represent, then I’m also supportive of that. But it seems that, including the President, many have agreed that an incentive would be the most constructive way to achieve this goal. But that having been said, I will never take any option off the table. I’m curious what you’ve heard from constituents in your district about the phenomenon of production moving out of the country and the impact it’s had on them. Well, frankly, many of those affected are people I interact with and engage and they’re now onto second, third or fourth careers, and the common theme across many of those interactions with my constituents is they wish they were back filming movies. And though I’ve never been involved in movie production, as somebody that’s been involved with politics for some time, I can understand the excitement that’s connected to making a film and seeing it on the big screen and having that pride and having a community be excited about some of the locations at which films were made. So I certainly hear it from my constituents as it relates to them wishing they could be back in the movie industry and wishing they had the stability that they enjoyed many years ago. And I’m eager to deliver wins for my constituents as any member of Congress should be. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal editorial board came out with a piece that questioned the tax incentive, calling it “handouts for Hollywood.” What is your response to this kind of criticism? Well, I certainly respect their perspective. I think that, as I mentioned before, an all-above approach is the most constructive way, I think. I should reread their editorial, but I suspect that they too share the objective that we all have, which is to ensure we have a robust film industry in America. We view that as a soft power export, a cultural export. We certainly want Americans to enjoy American film as they grow up just as you and I did when we were growing up. So I respect their perspective and ultimately we’ll watch this legislation continue to move and grow within the United States Congress. And ultimately I think it’s up to our constituents to convey to us what they determine as necessary for a robust film industry, especially in many of these districts where film has made a big impact. So I think you can go around each congressional district and see district impact by film production in previous years. Turning to the caucus now, I’m curious what some top items on the agenda might be for that group. Well, I think first and foremost, you’re going to see an effort to educate members about the benefit. We saw the study that you reported on yesterday. Those are very encouraging numbers, $250 billion projected over eight years to generate growth in the American economy, over 140,000 jobs to be created. And frankly, the best legislation comes out of very informed members of Congress debating issue sets. And we have thousands of issues on Capitol Hill in which we deal with every month. So I am eager to partner with our caucus members to educate members of Congress about the benefits of film production. And I can speak to it from my own congressional district as to how it’s been beneficial for my own. There are a lot of caucuses out there. What sort of pragmatic things can a caucus accomplish in this case? It can be an opportunity, especially as we break for the election, for members who are interested in the topic. The caucus is a wonderful way to learn more about the topic and we’ll have quite a few weeks before Congress returns to session. So I’m hopeful that members want to join the caucus or take interest in the caucus. And though there are many caucuses, the effectiveness rate of caucuses is usually connected to the engagement level from the leadership. How do you plan on convincing your Republican colleagues who may not come from states where there’s a ton of production to get behind this idea? First and foremost, I think the underlying effect on the economy, $250 billion over the next eight years if we see movement and action on this topic, is persuasive. I think the President has very much laid out the case as well that he thinks it’s a national security priority for us to ensure that American entertainment is made by Americans, filmed by Americans, produced by Americans. So I think there’s certainly an element of that as well, but ultimately it’ll be incumbent upon not just members of Congress that are interested in it like myself, but also it’s important for constituents to chime in. And by the way, I think if you go around many districts across the country, there are going to be stories — maybe it was 10 years ago, maybe it was 15 years ago — but a movie being filmed in a certain area, maybe that had a big impact that members of Congress today should know about. Favorite movie? The Godfather. Favorite TV show? Entourage. What are you watching right now, if you’re watching anything? Well, a lot of college football and a lot of professional football. I love The Odyssey . I saw it a few times this summer. I was going to ask; I read that you were a Christopher Nolan fan. Big time. I saw Spider-Man: Brand New Day , which was good. I’m not currently watching a show, but I often re-watch… if you’re inclined to include this, I was a massive fan of Lost way back when. But I saw By Any Means this past weekend, and I’m a big fan of Mark Wahlberg. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. THR

Fina Strazza stars as Billie Blake, who comes back to her hometown after her mother comes into a dress shop through an inheritance. Next door is a diner run by Calvin Wilkes (Brian Altemus), her boyfriend from high school. Thrown together with him again, Billie has to confront the honesty and the deception that brought their relationship to an end. Smulders won the 2017 Theatre World Award for her debut performance in Noël Coward’s “Present Laughter,” opposite Kevin Kline. “It’s great to get a chance to return to my stage roots with the pathos of this film, which started when I studied at Studio 58 in Vancouver, and of course at Second City,” Mochrie said. “Improv and theater are closely related, and there’s something incredibly exciting about bringing that experience into Rana’s world. title: ‘Ray Gunn’ Trailer: Sam Rockwell and Scarlett Johansson Star in Netflix’s Sci-Fi Murder Mystery From ‘Incredibles’ Director

It follows Raymond “Ray” Gunn (Sam Rockwell), a private eye detective, and Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), a pop star facing a scandal that could end her career — or her. title: Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs
full_text: Sep 23, 2026 6:16am PT Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Taylor Swift Announces ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ Album With Four New Songs 49 minutes ago Dolly Parton’s Manager Files for Restraining Order Against Fired Nephew, Alleging Ex-Security Head Sent ‘Terrorizing’ Texts and Threatened to ‘Destroy the Entire Brand’ 11 hours ago Taylor Swift Announces New Single, ‘Patient Zero,’ Coming This Week 20 hours ago See All TAS Rights Management No surprise here: “Patient Zero,” the song Taylor Swift announced Tuesday, is not an orphan or a one-off. The pop superstar followed news of the single a day later with her Wednesday morning reveal for a release that includes four new tracks and will also be out this Friday — “ The Life of a Showgirl : The Encore.” A visit to pre-order pages shows that the new songs, besides the already announced “Patient Zero,” are “Cleveland!,” “Pink Clouding” and “Babylon,” listed as tracks 13-16 on the newly expanded version of her 2025 “Showgirl” album. On social media, Swift wrote, “About a year ago, you guys did a truly unfathomable thing. Something that completely blew my mind… You gave ‘The Life of a Showgirl’ the biggest first week for an album in history. I took a trip to Sweden to celebrate with Max and Shellback , my two collaborators on this album. Really we just wanted to reflect and take in how grateful we were for the moment we were in, but there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: We wrote more songs. I hope you love them, because they were born out of pure gratitude for your exuberance for and celebration of the album we made. ‘The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore’ including four new songs is out on Friday and available to pre-order and save now.” Swifties had long assumed there would be no deluxe or bonus-filled edition of 2025’s “The Life of a Showgirl” because, at the time, Swift had assured fans that she felt pleased with the exact 12-song configuration she was putting out and did want to augment it with anything she might have left on the cutting room floor. But, as fans now learn, that didn’t preclude coming up with additional material after the fact, which the singer is saying came out in a spontaneous explosion of post-release exhilaration with her two collaborators on that album. View this post on Instagram Prior to “Showgirl,” she hadn’t worked with the dynamic duo of Max Martin and Shellback since 2018’s “Reputation,” but clearly the reunion took in a big way. Popular on Variety Related Stories Christina Applegate Shares First Video Following Months-Long Hospitalization: ‘Love to You All Out There’ Eagle-eyed Swifties noted that Swift had quietly teased this project some time ago, by including the phrase “Patient for the encore” to the side of the frame in her music video for the “Showgirl” single “Opalite.” Much more recently, she had given fans Easter eggs in puzzle form with a pre-taped sketch that aired as part of the Emmys telecast. There; Swift, in character as a “Law & Order: SVU” detective, said, “I think what we’re going to be looking for is hiding in plain sight.” She then stared into the camera and uttered several seeming nonsense phrases or words: “Saccharide. Aries. From the vineyard. North or south.” Fans eventually figured out that if you took the third letter from each of those utterances, they gave up the letters that form the word “encore.” The announcement of the “Encore” edition also settles another point of trivia that had come up when Swift revealed the “Patient Zero” single was imminent on Tuesday. Many pointed out that Swift was not lately in the habit of releasing a stand-alone single ahead of an album actually coming out; the last time she had done so was with “Me!” being released months ahead of “Lover” in 2019. Now that everyone knows the “Encore” collection is coming out the same hour as the single, it’s clear she’s not breaking with that recent pattern after all. The new release features cover photography by the team of fashion photographers Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott, continuing the imagery they created ffor the original “Showgirl” album. No physical release has been announced for the expanded project, which hits DSPs as Thursday night turns into Friday morning. The streaming service Apple Music does show the track list as being broken down into Disc 1 (the original 12 tracks) and Disc 2 (the four newly released songs), but it’s unclear if that augurs for a two-disc vinyl or CD edition. Spotify has the 16 tracks listed in a single running order. For now, the release of the four “Showgirl” addenda puts to bed previous widespread conjecture that Swift was certain to put out “Taylor Swift (Taylor’s Version)” this fall to celebrate the 20th anniversary of her debut album. But setting that aside for newly written songs is a tradeoff most fans will be happy with. So, “Our Song (Middle Aged Version)” can wait. title: Broadcast TV Bounces Back: More Orders as Network Fare Drives Streaming Ratings
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 6:15am Mike Colter and Rachel Keller in CBS' 'Cupertino.' Elizabeth Fisher/CBS Logo text The 21st century has not been terribly kind to broadcast TV. The DVR, a spike in cable original programming and, most recently and seriously, the rise of streaming to become the primary way people consume TV, have battered the network model for the past couple of decades. The stats don’t lie: Over the past year, broadcast networks have averaged only about 21 percent of all TV use in the United States, based on Nielsen’s Gauge measurement. The Oscars are moving to a streaming platform, and the Emmy Awards may follow. Late night shows are suffering deaths by a thousand cuts (or, in CBS ‘ case, one big one). Obviously, there’s a “but” coming, and here it is: Despite the structural forces weighing on the network business, there’s also a good deal of optimism among those who work there. Network shows don’t draw the on-air ratings they once did, but they make up a lot of the difference when they hit streaming platforms. The media giants that own both networks and streaming services seem to have figured out that the two platforms can support one another. And among the people who actually make the shows, there’s a growing sense that the network model of producing shows on a set schedule is a good way to do business. UTA partner and TV literary agent Mickey Berman, who represents several writers and showrunners, puts things pretty succinctly: “When you look at the combined package, the shows are working and people are watching them.” Part of the appeal of network TV, both for audiences and creatives, is its consistency: The expectation is that they’ll be on the air every year, usually with 12 to 22 episodes per season. The early years of the streaming boom promised a reprieve from the admittedly grueling schedule of a full network season — but as that model has moved from still fairly regular (if shorter) seasons to eight or 10 episodes every couple of years, the network model has come back into vogue (see also: The Pitt and HBO Max’s recently ordered How to Survive Without Me and FX and Hulu’s The Bear , among other streaming series that have approximated the network model). “I think for a while, people were a bit seduced by streaming and enjoyed some of the creative freedom and other things about it,” Lisa Katz, president scripted content for NBC and Peacock, tells The Hollywood Reporter . “But over time, broadcast shows have continued to show they’re consistent, and I think that they continue to be high in quality and bring in fans. There’s something about it — maybe the new thing felt great, but NBC is celebrating its 100th anniversary, and there’s a reason it’s had the staying power and the legacy that it has.” Berman also notes the “tremendous amount of stability” in working on a network series. For writers, actors, directors and other crew members, “They know that if a show works, they’re going to be shooting or writing for a certain period of time with more episodes and hopefully more seasons.” Michelle and Robert King, the creators and showrunners of The Good Wife, The Good Fight and CBS’ freshman drama Cupertino (among other shows), have moved back and forth between broadcast and streaming. The network business has its pluses, they say. “Selfishly, one thing about doing broadcast shows is they don’t get lost,” Michelle King says. “There are a few streaming shows that one hears about, but there are so very many that seem to just get lost that no one has heard of. Broadcast shows tend to get marketed. People have heard of them, and people get to see them. We’re super proud of Cupertino , so we’re thrilled that people are going to get to see it.” Robert King adds that he’s found — somewhat counterintuitively — that they have more control over a network show than they might on a streaming series. “You don’t have a lot of non-writing producers looking over your shoulder because of the speed with which everything needs to be done,” he says. “I mean, they talk about streaming doesn’t know how to do 20 episodes a year anymore. Writers do. It’s just the non-writing producers want to [sweat] everything. … I like doing 20 episodes because you can be intuitive in the writing and the stories you tell.” Amy Reisenbach, the president of CBS Entertainment who greenlit Cupertino , says she has fielded calls from creators and showrunners looking to return to a broadcaster after making streaming shows. “There is nothing like waking up the next day, from a writer’s perspective and executive’s perspective, in my mind, to getting the ratings and getting a [glimpse] into what you did last night,” she says. “And when you’re waking up to 8 million-ish viewers for Tracker and Marshals the next day … I don’t think you can underestimate the power in that and knowing how many people tuned in for your show the night before.” The stability of network TV extends to the number of scripted series at the networks as well: 56 shows are due to air on the big four broadcasters in the 2026-27 season, up from 50 (plus one limited series, Fox ‘s The Faithful ) last season. ABC , CBS, Fox and NBC combined canceled only six scripted series (ABC kept all 10 of its shows), while adding a dozen to their rosters. “There’s been a renewed interest from the talent base in broadcast because of the stability, because of the quicker turnaround, because of the opportunity for more episodes and more seasons, and that’s not just financial,” Berman says. “It’s also about building a relationship with the audience, where they fall in love with characters and can see them on a schedule that they expect. Grey’s Anatomy has been on the air for so long. People love those characters. But even [for shows that haven’t been on for as long], people want to grow with those characters.” NBC’s Katz also led the charge for a mini-revival of pilot season in the spring, making eight of them and picking up four (dramas Line of Fire and The Rockford Files and comedies Newlyweds and Sunset P.I. ). Networks continue to develop shows year-round and using various methods to develop shows, from smaller pre-pickup writers rooms to straight-to-series orders. But the pilot process has a lot of upside, from Katz’s perspective. “It benefits the show and gives us the opportunity to launch it in the most successful way possible, and to make some adjustments, whether it be in casting or a storyline, when we still have time to do it,” she says. “That’s one of the things I’ve loved about broadcast that’s really challenging in streaming. In streaming, the way that we’re doing it, you have maybe three weeks left of shooting when you’re seeing the first cut. It’s very hard to make adjustments.” One other key factor fueling the optimism around network shows is that in the past few years, media giants have recognized that broadcast and streaming can be complementary rather than mutually exclusive. That network shows bring in sizable audiences when they reach streaming is hardly new information, but better Nielsen measurement of streaming — and the public release of more data — has helped bring the point home. For the 2025-26 season, about half of the top 25 shows in cross-platform ratings originated on broadcast networks. Nine network series (not including sports and news programs) averaged 10 million or more cross-platform viewers, and four others came in just below that threshold. With ABC, CBS and NBC’s parent companies each owning a big streaming service (Hulu/Disney+, Paramount+ and Peacock, respectively), the broadcast-streaming symbiosis is good for both aspects of the business. (Fox has a next-day streaming deal with Hulu for its shows, and some are also available on its own platforms, free streamer Tubi and the year-old Fox One subscription platform.) “We have always considered Paramount+ and CBS parts of a larger ecosystem that includes Pluto as well,” Reisenbach says. “We have a great partnership with Cindy [Holland] and Jane [Wiseman]. They’re obviously working on their shows, which are very different than our shows, but we’re conscious of wanting to be complementary. I’m so appreciative of how grateful they have been for the next-day programming from CBS. They totally get what we do and the kind of shows that we make, and they have created this lane for us.” The network-streaming relationship and the uptick in series orders has Berman feeling good about the next couple of years for his clients, and for network TV. “I think in the next couple years, there’s going to be tremendous opportunity to capitalize on that [momentum], and hopefully new models come from that about how our clients participate,” Berman says. “I’m really optimistic. I feel like the worst is definitely behind us, and I’m glad we have a four-year [labor] deal so that we can really build some momentum toward the future.” THR

title: French Film & TV Sectors Sound Alarm Over Cuts To State Broadcaster Budget; Say They Are At Odds With Macron’s Lumière Summit Pledges
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie ‘Ray Gunn’ Trailer: Netflix Adds Limited Dec 4 Theatrical Release For Brad Bird’s Sam Rockwell & Scarlett Johansson-Voiced Animated Sci-Fi Studiocanal Announces Wrap Of Final Film In Ambitious German-Language ‘Woodwalkers’ Trilogy Oscars: Italy Submits Paolo Strippoli’s ‘The Spiral’ For Best International Feature Film View All September 23, 2026 6:05am French flag Getty Images France ’s film and TV sectors are sounding the alarm over a proposed €47M ($53M) cut in public funds for state broadcaster France Télévisions in 2027. In a joint open letter published on Wednesday, independent producers’ guilds, Le SPI, l’USPA and AnimFrance accused the government of engaging in “a brutal social plan” which could cause irreparable damage to France’s audiovisual sector. The guilds said the cuts also fly in the face of pledges made by President Emmanuel Macron at his Lumière Summit, unfolding in the South of France on September 7 and devoted to the future of the moving image, and its accompanying declaration highlighting “the vital role of the state” and the “audiovisual industry as an engine for economic growth”. “In the wake of the Lumière Summit, the first international summit dedicated to the future of cinema and the moving image, government decisions are set to plunge the entire sector into deep chaos: after affirming the strategic nature of the image industries and the importance of our cultural sovereignty, the government has chosen to undermine those who create, produce, and distribute these works,” read their letter. The open letter follows in the wake of an interview with France Télévisions President Delphine Ernotte Cunci in the ‘Le Monde’ newspaper on September 18, in which she said the state broadcaster was facing a €90M ($100M) cut in its budget for 2027. This was due, she said, to a proposed €47M ($53M) cut in state funds combined with a fall in advertising revenue and the impact of rising inflation. She noted that the state cut in funds for 2027 followed in the wake of a €80M cut for 2026. She said the funding situation risked destroying France’s cultural model. “I’m pulling the alarm to safeguard our cultural model,” she said. “What’s emerging is that the foreign platforms will soon account for the biggest investments in French creativity. “That means series and films will be greenlighted, financed, cast, written and conceived by the Americans and the Chinese. Do we want to weaken this industry of creation, of freedom, which employs more people than the car industry?” The proposed France Télévisions budget cuts are part of a larger €54B ($61B) package of spending cuts being put forward by the French government to rein in public debt, which it says is poised to hit a record 121.7% of domestic product (GDP) in 2027. “SPI, USPA, and AnimFrance are fully aware of the state of public finances and the need for everyone to contribute to the collective effort. However, this effort must be managed responsibly and be economically efficient,” the guilds said in their letter. “At a time when overall unemployment is rising alarmingly and recession is looming, the state, as shareholder of France Télévisions, has made a harsh and counterproductive budgetary decision: the planned cutbacks in public broadcasting risk producing the exact opposite of the intended result. This move deals a severe blow to the 700 production companies working with the public broadcaster and will inevitably cause unprecedented social damage within the audiovisual sector.” The guilds reiterated Ernotte Cunci’s comments on the audiovisual industry employing more people than the car industry in France. “The audiovisual sector accounts for 260,000 direct and indirect jobs across France and generates over €12 billion in added value, surpassing both the automotive and textile industries,” read the letter. It added that it was wrong to view state funding for France Télévisions uniquely through the lens of budgetary expenditure, saying it was also an investment. The guilds said that every euro in state funding went onto generate €2.40 within the French economy, with €0.50 of that “flowing back into state coffers”. “Reducing public funding will not result in equivalent savings for the state; instead, it will trigger a destructive downward spiral of fewer jobs, lower social security contributions, reduced tax revenue, and higher unemployment benefit payouts, ultimately yielding no real savings while leaving the country culturally impoverished,” read the letter. Related Stories Acquisitions Disney+ Seals EMEA Deal For Season 1 Of TF1 Hit 'Cat's Eyes' As Season 2 Gets October Launch Date News Oscars: France Selects 'Minotaur' For Best International Feature Film Race It added that the cuts came at an already difficult time for the audiovisual sector, due to fewer commissions from private broadcasters, the budgets of which have also been hit by falling ad revenue and inflation. Watch on Deadline “In practical terms, a further drop in orders and contracts resulting from public austerity measures will immediately impact production companies’ ability to sustain employment. Writers, directors, actors, and staff—whether permanent or on short-term contracts—represent a vast pool of skilled, high-value-added jobs that the proposed budget places in immediate jeopardy. This would mean the direct loss of nearly 10,000 jobs, on top of the 10,000 already lost since 2023,” read guild’s letter. In other woes, not detailed in the letter, figures released by film and TV export body Unifrance earlier this month revealed a collapse in international sales for French shows in 2025 to a ten-year low. Le Spi, Le SPI, l’USPA’s open letter, follows a similar statement published on September 18 in the immediate aftermath of Ernotte Cunci’s interview, from nine film and TV bodies including director’s guild L’ARP, distributors’ organisations DIRE and SDI as well as the screenwriters association SCA. They were equally scathing in their criticisms of the government’s proposed cuts, saying it would be a “devasting blow” for both the TV and cinema industries. The letter also took aim at Macron’s Lumière Summit, which gathered a host of U.S. studio and streamer heads and Hollywood stars in the South of France, while much of Europe’s independent international film sector was focused rather on the Venice Film Festival in Italy. Macron hosted the event jointly with Korean President Lee Jae Myung, with their respective countries pledging to invest 1 billion euros ($1.16 billion) in the global screen industries from 2027 to 2031. “While the President of the Republic was rolling out the red carpet for American platforms at the “Sommet Lumière” on September 7 and speaking of a “civilizational issue”, we learned just days later that public broadcasting faces unprecedented peril, and with it, our cultural sovereignty,” read their statement. “It is unacceptable for paid American platforms to become, in the near future, one of the primary financiers of French cinema. Audiovisual and cinematic creation is a strategic asset for France, yet this financial decision demonstrates that our government fails to grasp the magnitude of what is at stake. title: Cineplex Puts Up “For Sale” Sign as It Names New CEO
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All September 23, 2026 5:41am The main entrance of Cineplex's Scotiabank Theatre Toronto. Roberto Machado Noa/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Cineplex has put itself up for sale while unveiling former Landmark Cinemas head Bill Walker as its new CEO, replacing a retiring Ellis Jacob. “As part of the strategic review, the board will consider a range of alternatives, including, but not limited to, a potential sale of the company. The board has engaged Goldman Sachs and TD Securities as co-financial advisors in connection with the strategic review,” Cineplex, the Canadian exhibition giant, said in a statement via its board of directors. Cineplex operates around 1,606 movie screens at 156 locations across Canada, and is a major launchpad for Hollywood tentpoles and other films screening north of the border. Putting up a for sale sign gets Cineplex back to where it was the last time Jacob sought an exit from the exhibition giant in 2019. At that point, U.K. exhibition giant Cineworld Group unveiled a deal to acquire Cineplex for $2.1 billion to create a company with more than 11,200 movie screens globally. But a year later, as the pandemic took hold on the exhibition industry, Cineworld abandoned the movie theater deal to create one of the world’s largest cinema companies. Cineplex was subsequently awarded damages of $1.236 billion in lost synergies from the abandoned takeover deal, but was unable to collect those funds after Cineworld went through a Chapter 11 bankruptcy process in the U.S. That left Jacob and his executive team at Cineplex having to manage their balance sheet and greatly disrupted business in Canada during the pandemic. The latest attempt to possibly sell Cineplex comes amid better times for the Canadian exhibitor as it rides a Hollywood box office rebound. Jacob, a Canadian exhibition industry pioneer, in mid-2025 announced he will stay on at the movie theater chain until the end of 2016 to assist a transition to new leadership. That includes Walker being named as the new CEO. Walker previously served as CEO of Landmark Cinemas, Canada’s second-largest theatre exhibitor, which operates as part of Kinepolis Group NV, a publicly traded cinema company based in Belgium. Walker helped seal Landmark’s sale to Kinepolis in 2017, while continuing to run the company under Kinepolis’ public ownership. Jacob will become a special advisor to the Cineplex board as it looked to strategic alternatives to maximize returns to shareholders. “Bill brings a unique combination of industry expertise, operational leadership, transaction experience and strategic perspective. Given his deep understanding of the theatrical exhibition industry and proven leadership experience, the board is confident that Bill is exceptionally well positioned to lead Cineplex. At the same time, the board believes it is appropriate to conduct a comprehensive review of strategic alternatives available to the company,” Cineplex board chair Phyllis Yaffe said in a statement. Cineplex added no timetable for its strategic review process has been set as the company added “there can be no assurance” that a transaction will follow as the company continues to operate as usual. “Having spent much of my career in the exhibition industry, I have great respect for what the Cineplex team has built. I believe the company possesses an exceptional platform for growth, a powerful brand and meaningful opportunities to create value. I fully support the Board’s commitment to evaluating strategic alternatives and look forward to working closely with the board, management team and other stakeholders as the strategic review progresses,” Walker added in his own statement.
