title: Jesse Eisenberg Used to Have “a Negative Opinion” of Acting: “They Pay Us Too Much, We’re Vain”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 5:21am Jesse Eisenberg at the 2026 San Sebastian Film Festival Getty Images Spain Jesse Eisenberg regaled a room of journalists with brilliant — but slightly tragic — tidbits from his childhood and career while discussing his latest feature, The Debut . Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halle Bailey, Havana Rose Liu, Bernadette Peters, Colton Ryan, Lilli Cooper, Maulik Pancholy and Bonnie Milligan join Eisenberg in The Debut , following a shy woman (Moore) who is unexpectedly cast in a local production of an original musical. Under the spell of the strong-willed and enigmatic director (Giamatti), she loses herself in the role and the high-stakes world of this community theatre production. Related Stories Movies Brad Pitt Says Indie Cinema "Feels as Strong as in the '90s" Business MIP London Ends After 2 Years, Replaced by London Book Fair Event The film is premiering at the San Sebastian Film Festival , where an extremely polite Eisenberg (“thank you so much,” he said after each question) appeared for a press conference on Wednesday. The actor-writer-director, whose last film A Real Pain was nominated for multiple Oscars, said The Debut is partially autobiographical as it pulls on his own experience joining community theater. “The movie takes place in 1990 in central New Jersey, and when I was in central New Jersey in 1990, I was like [Moore’s character] Mona Friedman. I was so shy. I was depressed, and I didn’t have friends. And then I walked into this community theater when I was seven years old, and suddenly everybody was so nice, and they hugged me,” he said, prompting giggles from the room. “Going from a kid who was made fun of in school because I have the same hair as you, curly hair, and the kids were saying mean things to me. And then I walked into the community theater, and everybody said, ‘Wow, your hair is so amazing! Come this way, you should play with me!'” Jesse Eisenberg is asked why he chose not to reprise his role as Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s #TheSocialReckoning at the San Sebastian Film Festival: “It just didn’t feel like something I wanted to act in again. But that’s nothing to do with how great the movie is… Jeremy… pic.twitter.com/frYHOls2BF — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 23, 2026 The experience was, to say the least, transformative. “Suddenly it was like I walked into an alien planet where everybody was nice, and then just like Julianne Moore’s character, I took it too far and became crazy. So really, the movie is charting my life when I was a child. But I just thought it would be so much better to make it about an older woman because Julianne’s amazing, and it’s more emotionally impactful to see a woman.” Such is his admiration for Moore — who starred in Eisenberg’s first directorial feature, 2022’s When You Finish Saving the World — that she changed his long-held view of acting. “I used to have this negative opinion about acting because I was an actor and I just thought, ‘This is just such a ridiculous job. They pay us too much. We’re vain,'” said Eisenberg. “We want to look pretty in the morning, we want to stay in the nicest places, and we want to not ever lift anything on movie sets, and then we want all the credit for the movie! I was always like, ‘This is a weird job, and it’s not fair.’ And then on my first movie, I saw Julianne Moore rehearsing for a scene.” He saw her on the monitor, preparing for an office scene. “She was going through a real, deep emotional process to get ready for the scene. I remember looking at it, and I go, ‘Oh, wait a second, that’s really hard.’ Like we’re all out here joking, and I’m having a donut, and she’s in there suffering. I realized, ‘Oh, maybe acting is actually a really valuable thing. Maybe difficult. Maybe it’s challenging. Maybe it takes a lot. And suddenly, in [one] moment, my entire opinion on acting changed because I saw somebody else doing it, and it wasn’t just about me.” Moore and Giamatti, he said, are two of his favorite actors. “And the movie has this element of a romance, which was not in the script at all,” revealed Eisenberg about Giamatti’s onscreen magnetism. “His character is not supposed to be romantically charming. He’s more supposed to be scary and mysterious. But he just brought this warmth to it, and it plays great in the movie.” Naturally, the filmmaker was also asked about his refusal to return to the role of Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s hotly anticipated Social Network (2010) follow-up, The Social Reckoning , which will instead see Succession alum Jeremy Strong in the role. “It’s ironic because people associate me with this website, but they know way more about the website than I do, and I like to keep it that way,” replied Eisenberg about the Facebook founder. “I’ve talked about it a lot, and Aaron Sorkin’s talked about it a lot. I loved his script, and he’s a genius,” continued the star. “And the movie, I’m sure, is incredible. But for me, it just didn’t feel like something I wanted to act in again. But that has nothing to do with how great the movie is. The movie will be a great movie, and Jeremy Strong will be amazing in the movie. I’m sure. I just didn’t feel like it’s something I wanted to do again.” The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sept. 18-26. THR

title: ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Sacha Baron Cohen’s Character Reinforcing “Harmful” Racial Stereotypes
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Sacha Baron Cohen’s Character Reinforcing “Harmful” Racial Stereotypes John Cleese Accuses BBC Of “Social Engineering” After Cutting Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ Chapter One Producers Complete Management Buyout From Anonymous Content; Take Investment From Former Fifth Season CEO Chris Rice View All September 23, 2026 5:00am Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G Amazon MGM Studios EXCLUSIVE : As the self-anointed “voice of youth” in the late 1990s, Ali G was a British cultural sensation, parroted in school playgrounds and quoted in Parliament. But nearly 30 years on, Sacha Baron Cohen has been criticized for “microwaving a relic from a generation ago” with his unexpected decision to reboot the suburban rude boy. In interviews with Deadline, Black British comedians voiced dismay at Amazon MGM Studios ’ upcoming film Ali G: Who Iz I? , arguing that the character is no longer associated with its roots of satirizing white men trying to adopt Black street culture. Instead, they said Ali G perpetuates racial stereotypes, diminishes the Black experience, and appropriates culture in a way that is damaging to the Black community. Related Stories Casting Michelle Rodriguez Latest To Join Amazon MGM Studios' Romantic Comedy 'Egg Baby' Casting Nicole Wallace Joins Josh Heuston In Amazon MGM Romance 'Throttled' Baron Cohen and Amazon MGM Studios declined to comment, but Deadline spoke with Colton Dunn, one of three Black writers who worked on Ali G: Who Iz I? , who said he did not recognize the criticisms. He argued that Baron Cohen remains faithful to Ali G’s origins, adding that the jokes target the movie’s subjects rather than Black people. “From my point of view, Ali G is not a racist character. Ali G is a tool to expose racists,” he said. Watch on Deadline Dunn explained: “He puts himself in the most ridiculous situations, and he doesn’t do that because he’s racist. He goes into these crazy-ass places, places where people would kill him if they knew what was going down. I don’t think he’s doing that from a racist point of view. That’s why I signed on. I wouldn’t sign on to work with somebody that I thought was racist, that’s against everything that I’ve done.” The debate erupted after the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? went viral last month. Jack Black, Tom Brady and Diplo all endorsed the character’s return, but it also sparked an online campaign to get the movie shut out of British cinemas because Ali G perpetuates “harmful stereotypes.” The campaign looks set to fail (Vue is among the theater chains planning to screen Who Iz I? when Sony releases it in the UK on October 23), but its message resonated with some in the Black British comedy community. Gina Yashere , a standup who co-created and starred in CBS comedy Bob Hearts Abishola , accused Baron Cohen of ostensibly adopting Blackface and “cosplaying” as another race. “He’s not targeting white people,” she told Deadline. “People watching that character are going to laugh because it’s a caricature of Black people.” Curtis Walker, another standup who starred in BBC series Paramount City , said he found Ali G “degrading” and “disgusting,” adding that it was “sad” that Amazon MGM Studios was backing the character, rather than Black creators. Yashire and Walker first voiced their concerns 26 years ago, when they were interviewed by New Nation , a newspaper for Britain’s Black community. The criticisms then grew louder at the Ali G in Da House premiere in 2002, when protesters demonstrated in Leicester Square, waving placards comparing the comic creation to Al Jolson, the American entertainer who was famous for performing in Blackface. Baron Cohen was aware of the concerns at the time, not least because Walker confronted him at an industry event. Baron Cohen told WTF with Marc Maron in 2016 that he decided not to engage publicly with the critics, even though he considered himself “vehemently against any form of racism.” He has long asserted that Ali G wants to be Black, but his true ethnicity is intentionally ambiguous. “He’s not Black. He is delusional,” he told NPR’s Fresh Air in 2009. Yashire and Walker’s views are shared by younger Black comics in the UK. Dane Baptiste, creator of BBC shows Sunny D and Bamous , said Ali G created a “skewed idea of Blackness” in Britain, and his revival is akin to “microwaving a relic from a generation ago.” He told Deadline: “After Black Lives Matter and the brief humanization of Black people and Black creatives, it seems very dubious that we are now regressing back, not just five years, but 25 years, to bring back a character that was able to flourish because there were no accurate portrayals of Black Britishness on screen.” Mo Gilligan, one of the UK’s most successful comedians, picked up on this theme during a recent appearance on The Louis Theroux Podcast . The BAFTA-winner said the depiction of Ali G became very “normalized” in the UK and there was a sense among some in the Black community that “you were being laughed at, not laughed with.” Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G Athena Kugblenu, a BBC New Comedy Awards finalist, argued that the latest incarnation of Ali G has had to embrace more “acute” racial stereotypes, including dreadlocks and a rastacap, because his costume is no longer unusual amid the assimilation of Black culture over the past 30 years. “He’s an analogue character in a digital age,” she wrote in an Instagram post liked by fellow comics, including Living With Yourself star Aisling Bea. A source close to Baron Cohen denied that Ali G has dreadlocks in the film. Michael Eboda, the former New Nation editor and CEO of Powerful Media, added: “There are far more serious things in the world than Ali G. It’s just something that has had its time. It was there for a minute, and now it’s just a bit sad that he’s having to rehash it.” Colton Dunn, whose credits include Widow’s Bay and Key and Peele , found Ali G “hilarious” when he first encountered the character during high school. “We all felt we knew a guy just like Ali G. I don’t remember it being controversial at all,” he said. “I don’t know what the experience is like for the Black performers in Britain. I’m not going to speak on their experience and I respect their experience, but I also respect my experience.” Dunn declined to comment on specific scenes or storylines, but said Baron Cohen has been working on the movie for years and Ali G’s contemporary relevance has been honed alongside many collaborators. The film is expected to touch on issues including cancel culture and immigration, while also having “ridiculous, silly-ass fun,” according to Dunn. Peter Fincham, the British television producer who first gave Ali G a platform in topical comedy series The 11 O’Clock Show , told Deadline that he was fascinated to see how the character has moved with the times. He admitted, however, that if a young white comedian was creating Ali G today, “questions would be asked” by studios and broadcasters. “The culture has changed. Sacha’s a very smart guy and will be sensitive to that, and I’m sure it will be reflected in the film,” said Fincham, who co-hosts Insiders: The TV Podcast. ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Racial Stereotypes MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Plot New Event Judge Sets Settlement Hearing Date; Read Consent Decree; More Reax Tom Cruise Pic’s World Premiere Was A Royal Affair; Recap + Photos Read More About: 5 Comments

title: ‘Where’s Wanda’ Season 2: Watch Trailer For Apple TV’s Darkly Comic German Series From UFA Fiction
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Tubi’s Brett Takeshita Joins Canada’s Enlighten Content ‘Where’s Wanda’ Season 2: Watch Trailer For Apple TV’s Darkly Comic German Series From UFA Fiction ‘The Masked Singer UK’ Producer Argonon Names New CEO As Founder James Burstall Becomes Exec Chair View All September 23, 2026 5:00am EXCLUSIVE: Here’s the trailer for Season 2 of Apple TV ‘s German dark comedy Where’s Wanda? . The sophomore season starring Heike Makatsch ( Love Actually ), Axel Stein ( The Vault ), Lea Drinda ( The Gryphon ), Leo Simon and and Nikeata Thompson ( Späti ) debuts globally on October 21, and this is the exclusive trailer ahead of the launch. Episodes will drop weekly through December 9, as previous announced. The UFA Fiction German-language comedy-drama picks up after the events of the first season, which saw Carlotta and Dedo Klatt (Makatsch and Stein) searching for their lost daughter Wanda (Drinda). As the season opens, Wanda is seemingly caught red-handed standing over a dead body and is hauled off to jail. Related Stories News Studiocanal Announces Wrap Of Final Film In Ambitious German-Language 'Woodwalkers' Trilogy Casting Janeane Garofalo Reteaming With Ben Stiller On Apple TV Comedy 'Protective Custody' Carlotta and Dedo have to do everything in their power to prove her innocence and avoid losing her again, with their investigation taking them to the heart of their sleepy suburban town, Sundersheim. Watch on Deadline In the trailer we see a shaken Wanda in jail. The scene morphs back to the murder scene, as Wanda finds a body dead backstage at a funfair. As the curtains pull back, she is revealed standing over the corpse with a bloodied trophy in her hands as the audience gasps. From there, her parents hatch their crazy plan to set her free and reveal the killer. “We end Season 1 with Wanda returning to her family, which is a great relief for them,” said Where’s Wanda? exec producer Nataly Kudiabor in an exclusive interview. “We had already announced that Wanda will be in prison in Season 2, and that has a huge impact on the family,” she said. “They have just got their daughter back, and now they have to deal with what this will do to them. “It also affects the family’s position in Sundersheim. What are the neighbours thinking? What do the people in Sundersheim think? Is it right that their daughter is in prison? There are a lot of questions being asked.” Sam Riley, Alexandra Maria Lara, Harriet Herbig-Matten, Gisa Flake, David Schütter, Palina Rojinski Suzanne von Borsody, Kostja Ullmann, Devid Striesow, Frederic Balonier, Sascha Geršak, Torben Liebrecht , Aaron Maldonado-Morales and Anton Dreger are also cast in Season 2. Oliver Lansley created, written and executive produced season 2, alongside UFA Fiction co-Managing Director and executive producer Nataly Kudiabor and Oliver Ossege. The series was co-created and based on a story by Zoltan Spirandelli, though he was not involved in Season 2, we understand. Tobi Baumann and Christian Ditter. We sat down for an exclusive interview with Kudiabor this week, who said Drinda’s titular character would be far more present in Season 2. “We always felt that Wanda was the heart of the show, so we wanted her to return and to give her more screen time,” she said. “Lea Drinda is a fantastic actress, and this time she isn’t hidden away for several episodes – she is there from the beginning.” Kudiabor revealed there would be “surprises” for the audience. “We love our surprises. For example, new neighbours move in: the Kimballs, played by Sam Riley and Alexandra Maria Lara, who are internationally known. They are a couple in real life, and we cast them as a couple in the show, which I think was a great idea. They bring a new layer to the series.” She added there would be “more twists and turns,” saying: “Oliver is very good at leading the audience in one direction and then revealing something unexpected from another side. There are also lots of interesting new characters in Sundersheim whom audiences haven’t seen before.” Kudiabor said that if Season 1 was about “the search, the neighbours and everything people were hiding in Sundersheim,” Season 2 was about “what the crisis is doing to the family and how they rebuild afterwards.” Working with Apple TV Where’s Wanda? was the first German-language original to come from Apple TV, with the likes of Constellation and Berlin ER following later. Prior to the show’s launch, there was a feeling within the German television production community that the global streamer’s future in Germany hinged on its success, with several privately voicing the opinion to Deadline at the time. The Season 2 renewal was validation the dark comedy had cut through, and Kudiabor praised the collaborative nature of Apple’s execs, with UFA Fiction in regular communication with Jay Hunt’s London office throughout the process. She noted that having an English writer in Lansley was “really helpful” to the flow of the development. “We were very excited to make Apple TV+’s first German original,” she said. “It’s great to work for a streamer with so many excellent shows. I’m a big fan of Apple’s productions, and quality is very important to them. “They always challenge us to do our best in terms of storytelling and production value, and it’s a great experience to be challenged and to keep getting better. Sometimes you think you know best, but ultimately it’s teamwork.” She compared the first mover experience to that of Wiedemann & Berg when it made Dark as Netflix’s debut German original. “If you’re the first show in a market for a streamer, you have to learn how to work together,” said Kudiabor. “I imagine it was a similar experience for Netflix when it made Dark . In the second season, the process was extremely nice and easy because we already knew each other and understood how things worked. There was a lot of trust in us, which was really nice.” German market in flux UFA Fiction, known for the likes of the Deutschland and Ku’damm franchises, has been on a roll over recent years, with Wanda? and Prime Video YA smash Maxton Hall – The World Between Us driving its streamer slate, with the likes of Disney+ miniseries Sam – A Saxon and Netflix movie Rising High also cutting through. However, the Fremantle-owned company could be seen as an outlier in the German production market. Last week at Seriesly Berlin, much of the chatter was about a general lack of funding outside of the global streamers, and whether international co-production could fill the gaps. With the likes of Sky Deutschland exiting the originals market in the past half-decade, things remain tough. “Streamers and commissioners are flooded with good ideas,” said Kudiabor. “What do you need to stand out? We’re really trying to work on that. I’m not saying we achieve it all the time, but we’re giving it our best, and perhaps our work shows that this approach is working for us.” She attributed UFA’s hot streak on “a mixture of luck, timing, having the right talent and finding the right story,” and hinted at several upcoming projects. “At the moment, we’re working for Amazon, with two shows launching there,” she said. “We’re working with Disney and have some developments with them, and we’ve just worked with Apple. We’re also working with HBO, so there are a lot of opportunities. “But it’s also about excellence. We’re challenging ourselves to ask, before we go out: Is this really the best story we have? Is this the best talent? Is there something else we can do before we go shopping?” Kudiabor admitted the success of Maxton Hall , which became Prime Video’s most-watched international original series. “The first season was amazing, but I don’t think we expected such sensational success,” she said. “I loved the second season, but wait for the third – it’s even more mind-blowing. The fans are so engaged and give their feedback through social media, which is crazy. Our main actors are now big stars, and it’s really a ride. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime moment. When you go to the premieres, it feels like a real event: The fans are going crazy and they really want to be part of it.” As for the future, Kudiabor said UFA Fiction will look to work with more production companies across the Fremantle group, as TV consolidated giants look to use their assets to create co-productions. “I’ve been speaking with colleagues in the Netherlands, for example, because our markets are quite similar and they have great shows coming out there,” said Kudiabor. “We recently had a meeting here to look for a project we could make together, so we want to develop something jointly. We’re also speaking with some UK companies.” Meanwhile, UFA Fiction is hoping Apple sees a long-term future for Where’s Wanda? . “Creatively, we have lots of ideas, but of course I can’t speak for Apple,” said Kudiabor. “Right now, we’re just happy to be returning for a second season. We hope to excite the viewers, and then we’ll take it from there.” ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Racial Stereotypes MIP London Comes To An End After Two Years; Organizers Plot New Event Judge Sets Settlement Hearing Date; Read Consent Decree; More Reax Tom Cruise Pic’s World Premiere Was A Royal Affair; Recap + Photos Read More About: Comments

title: John Cleese Accuses BBC Of “Social Engineering” After Cutting Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’
full_text: Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake ‘Ali G: Who Iz I?’ Writer Defends Amazon Movie Amid Outcry Over Sacha Baron Cohen’s Character Reinforcing “Harmful” Racial Stereotypes John Cleese Accuses BBC Of “Social Engineering” After Cutting Blackface Sketches From ‘That Mitchell And Webb Look’ Chapter One Producers Complete Management Buyout From Anonymous Content; Take Investment From Former Fifth Season CEO Chris Rice View All September 23, 2026 4:33am 'That Mitchell And Webb Look' BBC Studios John Cleese is unhappy with the BBC for removing sketches from comedy series That Mitchell and Webb Look . The BBC confirmed earlier this week that jokes featured in David Mitchell and Robert Webb’s show had been cut ahead of it being restored to iPlayer for its 20th anniversary. As many as 11 sketches were removed, including a self-referential skit in which Mitchell and Webb joked about the appropriateness of Blackface while in Blackface. title: Brad Pitt Says Indie Cinema “Feels as Strong as in the ’90s”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 4:08am Brad Pitt hits the 2026 San Sebastian Film Festival. Getty Images Spain Ahead of what will likely be a rabid San Sebastian Film Festival premiere, Brad Pitt joined his Heart of the Beast director David Ayer for a press conference on Wednesday. Journalists and attendees swarmed the room at the town’s Kursaal Theater, where a jovial Pitt made his first San Sebastian appearance since the 2009 presentation of Inglourious Basterds alongside filmmaker Quentin Tarantino. He delighted reporters by touching on man’s bond with dogs, the consolidation of Hollywood and the current independent film climate. Related Stories Business MIP London Ends After 2 Years, Replaced by London Book Fair Event TV 'The Remarried Empress' Special Look: Shin Min-a, Ju Ji-hoon Preview Disney+'s Lavish K-Drama Pitt was swiftly asked about his producing outfit and what he makes of the indie film landscape. The star was buoyant: “I think the current setup has actually been really conducive to independent [films], in a really cool way because more eyes are getting on these projects. It feels even as strong as in the ’90s,” he said, before asking Ayer for his own opinion. Ayer chimed in: “I think there’s new pipelines of discovery out there, new auteurs. We have people coming in off YouTube or the internet,” he said, referencing young horror directors Curry Barker and Kane Parsons, “but now we’re seeing what I believe may be the ascent of it, as we find filmmakers in that space, but also as young people matriculate into the industry. They have much different tastes, and they grew up on a different sense of media than we did. So I’m actually very excited about the future and future opportunities and future stories that are going to be told.” Brad Pitt makes his San Sebastian Film Festival entrance ahead of the premiere of David Ayer’s #HeartoftheBeast pic.twitter.com/EC3XYDgMpv — The Hollywood Reporter (@THR) September 23, 2026 Pitt was asked straight out of the gate about the consolidation of Hollywood, with the Paramount-WBD merger looming and in a climate where the streamers reign supreme. “What I love about what streaming has brought to us is so many more opportunities for actors, writers, directors,” replied Pitt. “And because of that, we have a greater plethora of really interesting stories and really interesting talents, and that’s been amazing. Of course, we had a dip — and we’re seeing that come back; we’re seeing the communal experience being embraced again.” He continued: “But what happened is movies got so expensive. We always talk about this. The very big tentpole movies were able to recoup, and the more independent, lower-budget, or anything in the middle ground — anything from maybe 30, 40, 60 [million dollars] — has a really difficult time getting made, even movies like ours, because it’s very difficult for the studio to recoup that middle budget. […] I’m hoping these movies still have a lot [of support], because that’s usually where I end up most,” he laughed. “The middle ground.” Pitt was also asked about the emotional bond between his character, James, and the dog, Odin, and why those bonds are so important in real life. He replied: “[The characters] James and Odin are both extremely capable creatures. They’ve been trained. They’ve been hardened. They’ve been proven. But it was more their bond between each other […] we would fight more for another than we would even for ourselves, and that kind of care and love and loyalty kept them both points in our film, and I think that’s also true love. When I think of the darker days, certainly my close relationships, I relied heavily on friends, dear close friends, handful of close family, and was very open about my growth.” For the final question (it’s a room full of European journalists, after all), Pitt was asked about how it’s possible to cope in a “sad world full of hate, wars, politics, and racism.” The U.S. star replied: “I think we could spend more time on where we are the same… What binds us, what connects us, and I think we can listen better through these divisional lines. But you know, maybe we just start taking care of the people that are around us and making sure they’re okay.” In Heart of the Beast the Oscar-winning star plays a former Special Forces officer who, accompanied by his retired combat dog, must survive in the Alaskan wilderness following a harrowing plane crash. Ayer’s credits include Training Day , Suicide Squad , End of Watch , The Tax Collector and Sabotage . His latest feature is written by Cameron Alexander and reunites him with Pitt (who starred in Ayer’s Fury ). The film’s cast also includes J.K. Simmons and Anna Lambe. Pitt produces the film alongside Olivia Hamilton, Marty Bowen and Ayer, with Damien Chazelle among its executive producers. The 2026 San Sebastian International Film Festival runs Sept. 18-16. THR

title: MIP London Ends After 2 Years, Replaced by London Book Fair Event
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 23, 2026 2:22am MIP London in 2025 Courtesy of Getty After two years, MIP London has ended and is set to be replaced by a new two-day conference taking place during the London Book Fair. On Wednesday, RX France confirmed the launch of MIP Talks from Mar. 16-17, 2027. The event will be backdropped by the London Book Fair, one of RX’s flagship events, bringing together leading voices from across the worlds of entertainment, media and culture to explore what is changing, what is breaking through and where new opportunities are emerging. MIP Talks will take place at London ExCel and is set to represent a “new expression of MIP in London, looking beyond traditional television and content to the wider cultural, creative, technological and commercial shifts reshaping global entertainment,” according to organizers. The inaugural MIP Talks will be built around the editorial theme ‘From IP to Fandom — and Fandom to Global Business,’ in which experts will explore an entertainment landscape where traditional boundaries are disappearing, audiences move across platforms and experiences, and IP can come from anywhere. Programming will be highly curated and editorially led, organizers added, spanning headline conversations, unexpected pairings, global trends and data, cultural insight and case studies from across the international entertainment business. Lucy Smith, director of the entertainment division, RX France, said: “The boundaries of entertainment have all but disappeared. IP can come from anywhere, audiences don’t think in sectors and an idea can travel further and faster than ever before. MIP has always been about understanding where the entertainment business is going next. MIP Talks at The London Book Fair takes that curiosity further bringing together the people shaping what breaks through, how fandom is built and where new global businesses are emerging.” THR

title: Donald Trump Just Told Ari Emanuel He’s Excited About a Vance-Rubio Ticket in 2028
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All September 23, 2026 12:47am Rachel Maddow grills Ari Emanuel at 92Y on Tuesday September 22, 2026 in New York Steven Zeitchik Donald Trump doesn’t want to stay in the White House past 2028, Ari Emanuel says — he’s too excited about JD Vance and Marco Rubio coming in instead. “I spoke to him three weeks ago,” the TKO chief told Rachel Maddow at New York’s 92Y Tuesday night, describing a call with the President about the federal tax credit. “And in that conversation … He thought JD and Marco Rubio would be a formidable group.” You mean as a joint ticket (presumably with Vance at the top), Maddow asked? “Yes,” Emanuel said. “That’s what he thought.” The best cable-news show Tuesday night wasn’t on the air. It was inside the New York venue, as Maddow interviewed her agent on the day of his memoir’s release, and despite their association repeatedly held his feet to the fire on a range of political and cultural topics. The (unstreamed) conversation went from convivial to feisty to testy and back again, as Emanuel sought to convince the audience, only sometimes successfully, that his friendliness with the White House and oligarchs like Elon Musk was for the greater good. “I don’t think it’s productive to say I’ve never changed him,” Emanuel said of Musk. “I do think I’ve changed him a little.” (Emanuel is notably friendly with Elon Musk, his company even investing in Musk’s Twitter.) Emanuel’s Roll the Calls tracks his time from a young apprentice in the CAA mailroom to his current status, at 65, atop the agency and UFC-WWE heap, with all the rage he (proudly) unleashed to get there. But at the event he showed a cannier side, one willing to play nice with power, as Emanuel praised moguls like David Ellison — whom the agent very publicly supported in his successful bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery. Though Emanuel allowed that he didn’t like how Paramount’s Stephen Colbert cancelation went down, he pointed to how Ellison has “let Matt and Trey do what they’re doing, and Jon do what he’s doing,” referring to South Park and The Daily Show , which regularly take aim at the President. “That’s like a cop pulling you over and you saying, ‘Look at all the people in the crosswalk I didn’t hit!’” Maddow said. “I appreciate the metaphor but I disagree with you,” Emanuel replied, as he talked up the (much-eyerolled ) oversight board charged with ensuring CBS News and CNN independence. “Do you worry about compliant billionaires taking over media?” Maddow asked. “You’re getting most of your news from your phone and social media,” Emanuel said, avoiding the question. Maddow was not done, noting how Ellison has “tanked the [CBS] morning show, the nightly news and is deep-frying 60 Minutes .” She called “the CBS News and 60 Minutes situation under Ellison” an “embarrassment.” She said she knew that for Emanuel there were “business reasons [to support the mogul] — he paid $8 billion to get UFC rights.” “7.4,” Emanuel corrected. “I wish it was eight.” The two spent some time in a lighter mode talking about such topics as Emanuel’s unusual longevity plays that has him doing cold plunges and eating live worms. (No, really.) But then one of the pricklier exchanges emerged when Maddow pressed the TKO leader on his 2018 meeting with Vladimir Putin (over potential UFC initiatives in Russia) and warming again to Saudi crown prince MBS after previously returning a $400 million investment in the wake of the Jamal Khashoggi murder. “Where’s the line?” Maddow asked Emanuel. “I’m sorry to say we’re adults … It’s not always black and white,” Emanuel responded, saying that he thinks MBS has now “done some incredible stuff.” “You’re getting frustrated,” Maddow said. “I’m not frustrated,” Emanuel replied, seemingly a little frustrated. Emanuel also defended his decision to hold a UFC event on the White House lawn in June (“there were incredible videos on American history”) and doubled down on Musk. “I don’t agree with Elon [on immigration],” Emanuel said. “On the other hand I was happy what he did in Ukraine blocking the Russians , happy what he’s doing with Neuralink, happy what he’s doing in space,” he said. Despite the support for some of the biggest business players around, Emanuel couldn’t resist a shot at the brass of rival CAA. “They have not handed the reins down,” he said of the top leaders, which includes Bryan Lourd, Kevin Huvane and several other longtime execs. “That’s bad leadership.” Emanuel also sought to downplay the singular threat of Trump’s presidency. “You don’t think people said at the time Nixon was the most dangerous president in all of U.S. history?” Emanuel asked, to demurrals from Maddow and some in the audience. “Shut the fuck up, stop,” he said, half-smiling. “He’s a different kind of cat,” Maddow pushed back on Trump, noting her belief that “I don’t think he’s going to leave [in 2028].” Emanuel said the Vance-Rubio comment indicated to him “that’s not a man trying to be in the White House forever.” (Rubio, incidentally, has indicated he won’t challenge Vance, which could pave the way to a VP selection. Of course, Vance would first have to win the nomination in what is expected to be a competitive primary, then deem Rubio enough of an asset in a post-Trump world to choose him. Also, an outgoing president hasn’t successfully joysticked the new one since the 1980’s.) Meanwhile, Emanuel’s own family may also be a factor in the race as Rahm Emanuel potentially positions himself to play centrist spoiler on the Democratic side. The younger Emanuel did nothing to cool the speculation about his brother when he said he would do “whatever I can” should he try to run, because “he’d be a great candidate,” as he talked up the former White House chief of staff and Chicago mayor. “Is there anybody more qualified than my brother?” Ari Emanuel asked. Maddow seemed most upset by Emanuel cozying up to Trump and oligarchs for what she suggested was his own benefit. “Is there anything about your relationships [with them] that has ever had a positive or mitigating effect on the harm they are doing to our country?” she asked. “I want to live in a society. You have conversations [in a society],” Emanuel answered. “When I’ve disagreed with the president, with Elon Musk, with a lot of the people you’ve mentioned, I have in my opinion swayed them. That might not satisfy you. I’m sorry,” he said. THR
